boxes.text: jit.p-vishnu;pos: position in 3-space;force: a bit like the 'wind' blowing in the space;pitch: front/back rotation;yaw: left/right rotation;speed: initial speed of emission;_var: variability;

Data emitted by p-shiva is n-plane, float32 or float64, 2 dimensional, x by 2. x represents the total number of particles permitted in any frame. Planes 0 and 1 always represent the particle id and life, respectively.

Data received by p-vishnu is expected to be 5 or 8 plane, float32 or float64, 2 dimensional, x by 2. If 5-plane, planes 2, 3, 4 represent x, y, z positions. If 8-plane, planes 5, 6, 7 additionally represent x, y, z velocities. When in mode 0, these extra planes are automatically generated for incoming 'newborn' particles'. In mode 1, any existing values in these planes are used to initialize the output.
turn toggle on and then play with these!
mode 1 enables 'init' and 'init_var' messages to affect p-shiva's output, and causes p-vishnu to use those values when 'launching' a new particle into the world.
Row 2 always holds the immediately previous value of row 1.
Instead of using jit.p-vishnu, you might simply use jit.op to create 'forces' to act on your initialized particles.
jit.p-shiva;life: particle life;emit: particles emitted per frame;_var: variability;

jit.p.vishnu is a single-force world simulator. So, it manages the emitter -- in what direction, and how fast, the particles are emitted, and also controls the "wind" in the world -- where the particles are blown to after they're emitted.;;Suppose you want to create a world that's not governed by "wind", but rather by a single attractive force. Instead of jit.p.vishnu, you will want to set up some math that pulls the particles in toward 0. Here's a simple example that uses jit.p.shiva's mode 1 (which allows you to generate initial positions for the particles using the 'init' and 'init_var' attributes), and jit.op to create a somewhat boring black hole, but it should get you started.

Planes 0 and 1 are particle ID and age, respectively. In genereal, you shouldn't touch them (note the 'pass' planar operator for those planes in the jit.op object). The remaining 30 planes can be used for anything. In most cases, assuming that you're using particles to represent something you want to render, you'll use planes 2, 3 and 4 to store x, y and z positions.

Incidentally, jit.p.vishnu will also understand 8-plane matrices, in case you want to manually adjust velocity (so, 5, 6, and 7 are vx, vy, vz in that case), but you could conceivably store and modify any number of non-spatial parameters in the additional planes.;;Additionally, although it's not shown here, init will take up to 30 args, one for each writeable plane). You can then use mode 1 to generate large, multiplane particle matrices.

The Jitter particle system is rather open-ended. Basically, jit.p.shiva is the birth/murder object. You give it the size of the particle set (dim), a rate of emission (emit) + variability (emit_var), the life-span of the particles (life) + variability (life_var), and it will automatically, each frame, do the right thing in terms of creating new particles or killing off old ones (it assigns new particles an id and a lifespan, and then checks that the particle is supposed to remain alive). You create a feedback loop in Jitter, using named matrices so that the same matrix of particles is repeatedly processed, dead particles are culled and new particles are born. The matrix produced by jit.p.shiva is an N x 2 matrix, where N is the size of the particle set. The top row is the current state of the system. The second row is the immediately previous state of the system (useful for calculating velocity).
